vasca_operation: Convoys move west overnight. The government does not confirm an operation in {region}, which is confirmation enough.
Roadblocks appear on the western approaches; nobody in {region} needs to be told what for.
vasca_amnesty: Terms are published for anyone who comes down out of {region} by spring. One name is conspicuously absent from them.
An amnesty is offered to the rank and file in {region} — everyone, that is, except the man they followed.
vasca_captured: Dorin Vasca is in custody. The first photograph shows a tired man in a borrowed coat, and half of {region} refuses to believe it is him.
They have Vasca. After fourteen months of rumour, {region} wakes up to a man in a cell and no idea what to feel about it.
vasca_isolated: The fighting in {region} has stopped without anyone declaring it over. What is left up there is a handful of men and an old grievance.
Whatever Vasca still commands in {region}, it is no longer enough to be called a movement.
vasca_dead: Dorin Vasca is dead. The government says he was killed in the assault; his people say he was alive when they took him. Neither account will ever be settled, and {region} has already chosen which one it believes.

Vasca did not survive the compound. There are two versions of the last twenty minutes, and the only men who could reconcile them are all on one side of it. {region} will argue about this for a generation.
vasca_exiled: Vasca leaves on a chartered flight before dawn, having read a statement he did not write. {region} watches it on television in silence.
The plane goes; the man goes with it. Somewhere in {region} they are still saying he will be back, and they may not be wrong.
vasca_unresolved: The compound is watched and nothing is done. Dorin Vasca goes to bed a free man in {region} for another night, and the government has no plans to change that.
The road stays under observation and the question stays open. {region} remains, for practical purposes, somebody else's country.
vetrenka_incident: Shelling on the contact line before dawn, an hour of it, and by breakfast each side has published its account of who fired first. {region} counts one dead and files a protest with the monitors.
The prisoner lists are exchanged again and again they do not match. Forty-one names on ours that are not on theirs; the delegation on the {region} side calls it an administrative discrepancy.
A Krasovan convoy in peacekeeper white takes the coast road through {region} — a road the ceasefire map does not give them. Nobody stops it. Somebody photographs it.
A drone, or a bird, or nothing at all over the {region} line at 0400, depending on which ministry you ask. The batteries were live for nine minutes.
vetrenka_talks: Ardenia takes a seat at the table. The delegation flies out under a formula that permits everyone to deny they are negotiating over {region}.
Talks open on the {region} question — the first time in a year that the word talks has been said aloud on the record.
vetrenka_offensive: The reserve call-up notices go out overnight. Whatever the ministry says at noon, the country understands by morning that {region} is going to be settled by other means.
Armour moves toward the {region} corridor. The government's statement uses the phrase restoring constitutional order, which is what statements say when a war is starting.
vetrenka_settled: The framework on {region} is initialled. Neither delegation says the word status; both go home able to claim they refused to. The shooting stops all the same.
It is signed. {region} is not returned and not conceded, and the paragraph that manages to be both is the finest piece of drafting anyone has seen in a decade.
vetrenka_talks_failed: The {region} talks collapse. The photograph that runs everywhere is of the empty table, and a year of the government's authority went into that room and did not come out.
No agreement on {region}. Each delegation blames the other's sequencing; the line goes back to what it was, colder, and next time the mediators will call somebody else.
vetrenka_retaken: Ardenian troops are in the regional capital. The flag goes up over {region} for the first time since 1992, and a third of the people who lived there have gone the other way.
{region} is retaken in nine days. The pictures are of the flag; the problem, starting tomorrow, is everything the pictures do not show.
vetrenka_rout: The offensive breaks. Krasovan aircraft are over the {region} corridor within the week, protecting peacekeepers by a definition nobody was consulted on, and the line is further inland than it was.
It failed. {region} is not merely still gone — it is bigger than it was, and a ceasefire is being offered on terms worse than the one this government turned down.
vetrenka_partition: The customs posts on the {region} line become permanent and the crossing publishes opening hours. No treaty is signed, no word is said, and the maps go to the printers with a dotted line on them.
Quietly, without ceremony and without the word recognition ever being used, {region} stops being a war and starts being a border.
vetrenka_normalised: The {region} crossing opens on schedule for the fifth month running. Nobody has forgiven it; everybody has stopped organising against it, which is the only kind of settlement this question was ever going to get.
Day permits, published hours, lorries queuing in the rain. The {region} line has become a timetable, and a timetable is very hard to hold a rally about.
vetrenka_backlash: The opposition has found its question — who gave {region} away — and it is on every leaflet, at every rally, and put to every minister who steps outdoors. There is no rebutting it, because the answer is the government.
Veterans' associations march over {region}, and behind them walk people who voted for this government. The campaign has one question in it and the government is the answer.
